To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) LAS is the main synthetic anionics surfactant found in sewage sludge, and (ii) its occurrence in sludge is due to its anaerobic persistence.

1) LAS and soap are found in sewage sludge at concentrations higher than the proposed European cut-off limit; 2) LAS is readily biodegraded under anaerobic conditions; 3) Soap is not readily biodegraded anaerobically and its presence in sludge is not explained by anaerobic biotransformation; 4) The proposed European cut-off limits for organic chemicals in sewage sludge should be based on the anaerobic degradability.

the average concentration of LAS in Spanish anaerobic sewage is 8.06g/kg, higher than average European values, and the implementation of the cut-off limit for LAS would render most Spanish sewage sludge not suitable for agricultural applications.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a critical analysis of the proposed limit for LAS in sewage sludge.
the need for the sewage sludge disposal to be considered in an integral way.
a critical evaluation of the European Sewage Directive and its implications for the management of sewage sludge.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed LAS limit in sludge is not appropriate to protect the environment, since most of the sludge would not comply with the limit and, therefore, would not be allowed for agricultural use.
the implementation of the LAS cut-off limit would not be justified in the European sewage sludge Directive.
the implementation of the proposed cut-off limit for LAS in sewage sludge would not guarantee environmental protection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of sludge for agricultural applications should be limited in order to prevent harmful effects in the environment.

the disposal of sewage biosolids to agriculture is not a safe way for the environment and that the European sludge directive should be reviewed to prevent the use of sludge with high levels of LAS and other chemicals in agriculture.
the use of sewage sludge for agricultural applications is not compatible with the implementation of a cut-off limit for the anionic surfactent LAS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a cut-off value for LAS in sewage sludge should be avoided, as it may have negative consequences for sludge disposal in agriculture.
the cut-off limit for LAS in sludge should be reconsidered, taking into account the high concentration of LAS and soap found in Spanish sludge.

the implementation of the cut-off limit for LAS in sewage sludge would make the disposal for agricultural applications of most Spanish sludge almost impossible, which would have a negative environmental impact, as it would increase the amount of sewage sludge disposed in other ways, such as landfills or incinerators.
